rationale: While early and Western multi-center cohorts identify muscular hypotonia (up to 60-62%) and behavioral dysregulation (62-85%) as frequent co-occurring manifestations of FBXO11-related neurodevelopmental disorder (IDDFBA, OMIM #618089), this signature fails as an invariant discriminator. Most notably, in a cohort of 12 Chinese affected individuals (Pan et al., 2024), hypotonia was documented in only 1 of 12 patients (8.3%), demonstrating substantial penetrance variability across cohorts and genetic backgrounds. Furthermore, in cohorts reporting high hypotonia frequencies, around 38% to 40% of patients do not exhibit hypotonia or behavioral disturbances, indicating that the absence of either finding cannot reliably exclude FBXO11-related disorder or serve as a standalone diagnostic signature without comprehensive molecular testing.

evidence.text: In a study of 21 newly reported individuals with FBXO11 variants, hypotonia was documented in 62% and behavioural dysregulation was present in 62%, making them among the most common manifestations alongside mild ID (86%) and facial dysmorphism (67%).

source.title: Defining FBXO11-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder: Clinical, Molecular and Facial Assessment of 21 Patients
source.quote: Mild intellectual disability (86%), facial dysmorphism (67%), hypotonia (62%), and behavioural dysregulation (62%) were the most prevalent features.

evidence.text: In an investigation of 24 individuals harboring de novo FBXO11 variants, behavioral disturbances (including ADHD, ASD, anxiety, aggression) were documented in most individuals alongside neuromuscular features including hypotonia and joint hyperlaxity.

source.title: De novo variants in FBXO11 cause a syndromic form of intellectual disability with behavioral problems and dysmorphisms
source.quote: All individuals had borderline to severe ID and behavioral problems (autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, aggression) were observed in most of them. ... Other features were hypotonia and hyperlaxity of the joints.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 12 Chinese patients with FBXO11 variants across 5 families, hypotonia was observed in only 1 of 12 individuals (8.3%), contradicting the expectation that hypotonia is consistently present in >60% of affected individuals.

source.title: FBXO11 variants are associated with intellectual disability and variable clinical manifestation in Chinese affected individuals
source.quote: In our affected individuals, hypotonia was observed in only 1/12

evidence.text: Among 20 individuals with de novo FBXO11 mutations, behavioral problems were documented in 17 of 20 (85%), while hypotonia and skeletal features were present as variable non-universal findings.

source.title: De novo variants in the F-box protein FBXO11 in 20 individuals with a variable neurodevelopmental disorder
source.quote: They present with mild to severe developmental delay associated with a range of features including short (4/20) or tall (2/20) stature, obesity (5/20), microcephaly (4/19) or macrocephaly (2/19), behavioral problems (17/20), seizures (5/20)

conflicts: Hypotonia prevalence varies sharply between cohorts, ranging from 60-62% in Goel et al. (2026) and Jansen et al. (2019) down to only 1 of 12 (8.3%) in Pan et al. (2024).
Neither hypotonia nor behavioral disturbances are fully penetrant (both ~62% in Goel et al.), meaning substantial subsets of FBXO11 patients lack one or both features.

new_directions.question_text: Does the prevalence of hypotonia in FBXO11-related disorder depend on variant position (e.g., CASH domain vs. UBR domain vs. truncating variants)?
new_directions.rationale: Gregor et al. (2022) revealed domain-specific functional consequences on protein localization and degradation, which may correlate with the presence or absence of neuromuscular features like hypotonia.

new_directions.question_text: Is the low reported frequency of hypotonia in certain cohorts (e.g., Pan et al., 2024) an artifact of ascertainment at older ages or a true population/variant-specific divergence?
new_directions.rationale: Congenital hypotonia often improves with age into childhood/adulthood; retrospective phenotyping in older cohorts may under-ascertain early-life hypotonia.
